title: Practice Set 7 — Data Pipelines: Orchestration in Fabric
description: Orchestrate NordGrid's data flow with Fabric Data Factory pipelines: match each NordGrid task to the correct activity type, predict Copy activity configuration fields, write a parameterized notebook that uses pipeline parameters, predict pipeline run outcomes when activities succeed or fail, choose the right trigger schedule for each data flow, and design NordGrid's complete daily ingestion pipeline as a structured specification.
version: authored 2026-04-06, targets Microsoft Fabric GA 2025+ / PySpark 3.5+

metadata.scenarioScale: 500K meters, 4 regions, single team, 3 medallion workspaces
metadata.foundationException: Not applied. F7 is Essential Operations phase. Fabric pipelines are configured in the portal canvas (a UI-heavy experience), not through code, so most tasks in this practice set use templates to test understanding of activity types, dependency logic, scheduling, and Copy configuration. The one code task (F7-task-03) tests the notebook-side of pipeline integration: how a parameterized notebook consumes parameters passed by a pipeline's Notebook activity (Lesson 8). The synthesis task (F7-task-06) uses pure Python dictionary construction to specify the complete NordGrid daily pipeline structure — no Fabric runtime is required. Task type mix (2 concept_identification + 2 output_prediction + 1 write_the_code + 1 synthesis_pipeline) is within §4.2 per-type limits.

datasets.description: NordGrid meter readings spanning 3 days (2026-03-08, 2026-03-09, 2026-03-10) with 5 rows per day across 4 regions. 15 rows total. Used in Task 3 to test parameterized filtering — the student receives a processing_date and region_filter as simulated pipeline parameters and produces a filtered DataFrame.

tasks.title: Match NordGrid's Steps to the Correct Activity Type

description.context: Fabric Data Factory pipelines are built from ACTIVITIES — one purpose per activity, chained together in the canvas. The five most common at Junior level: COPY ACTIVITY moves data from a SOURCE to a SINK without transformation (file-to-file, DB-to-Lakehouse, etc.). NOTEBOOK ACTIVITY runs a Fabric notebook (PySpark/SQL) — for code-driven transformations. DATAFLOW ACTIVITY runs a Dataflow Gen2 (Power Query Online) — for low-code transformations. WEB ACTIVITY calls an HTTP endpoint — for notifications and external integrations. SEND EMAIL ACTIVITY (Office 365 / Outlook connector) sends notification emails. Choosing the right activity means matching the action verb (move / transform-with-code / transform-low-code / call-HTTP / notify) to the activity's job.
description.task: For each NordGrid pipeline step, select the correct activity type.
description.validationHint: Copy activity = data movement from a source to a destination (no transformation). Notebook activity = run PySpark code in a Fabric notebook. Dataflow activity = run a Power Query Online (Dataflow Gen2) transformation. Web activity = call an external HTTP endpoint. Send Email activity = notify on success or failure.

fields.label: Move today's meter reading CSV from NordGrid's external SFTP server into the Bronze Lakehouse's Files section. No transformation — just copy the file as-is.
options: Copy activity — purpose-built for SOURCE-to-SINK file movement (SFTP to Lakehouse Files), no transformation, native auth and retry. Right tool for as-is copy.
Notebook activity — start a Spark session, write PySpark to read SFTP via paramiko, write to Files. Code-driven for full control.
Dataflow activity — Dataflows can read SFTP via Power Query connector, then write to a Lakehouse table.
Web activity — call the SFTP server via HTTP and store the response body in the Lakehouse.
fields.correctAnswer: Copy activity — purpose-built for SOURCE-to-SINK file movement (SFTP to Lakehouse Files), no transformation, native auth and retry. Right tool for as-is copy.
fields.rationale: External file movement with no transformation is exactly Copy activity's job. The most common Junior confusion is reaching for a Notebook (familiar) or Dataflow (visually appealing) when Copy is the purpose-built tool with native SFTP support, retry policy, and pipeline observability.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Notebook is overkill for a no-transform copy.

Option C: Dataflow is for transformation, not raw movement.

Option D: Web is HTTP only, not SFTP.

fields.label: Run NordGrid's Bronze-to-Silver transformation notebook, which performs schema enforcement, filtering, deduplication, and writes a partitioned Delta table.
options: Copy activity — Copy can carry transformation logic via mapping expressions and supports Delta as a sink format.
Notebook activity — runs the Fabric notebook with the PySpark transformation code (schema enforce + filter + dedup + Delta write). The only activity that executes a notebook.
Dataflow activity — translate the PySpark validation logic into Power Query and run it as a dataflow refresh.
Send Email activity — email-trigger the engineer to manually run the transformation.
fields.correctAnswer: Notebook activity — runs the Fabric notebook with the PySpark transformation code (schema enforce + filter + dedup + Delta write). The only activity that executes a notebook.
fields.rationale: Running a Fabric notebook from a pipeline = Notebook activity. The most common Junior confusion is conflating Notebook activity (executes a notebook) with the notebook ITSELF (contains the code) — they are two layers: the pipeline orchestrator triggers the notebook activity, which runs the notebook.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Copy is for movement; can't run PySpark.

Option C: Dataflows can't host PySpark.

Option D: Send Email notifies, doesn't run code.

fields.label: Refresh the 200-row substation reference table from an external SQL database: the flow must rename two columns, change one type, and write to a Lakehouse table. The data team prefers a low-code tool because the transformation is simple.
options: Copy activity — Copy supports column-level mapping including rename and type change as part of the source-to-sink flow.
Notebook activity — Spark gives full flexibility for the rename and type cast.
Dataflow activity — runs a Dataflow Gen2 (visual Power Query) that does the rename + retype low-code, writes to Lakehouse table. Built for this exact pattern.
If Condition activity — branch the pipeline based on whether the source table has changed since last refresh.
fields.correctAnswer: Dataflow activity — runs a Dataflow Gen2 (visual Power Query) that does the rename + retype low-code, writes to Lakehouse table. Built for this exact pattern.
fields.rationale: Small reference refresh + simple transformations + low-code preference = Dataflow activity (running a Dataflow Gen2). The most common Junior confusion is hoping Copy activity can do rename/retype; Copy supports basic column mapping but is not the right tool when a few transformation steps are needed.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Copy supports basic mapping; it's not the low-code-transform tool.

Option B: Notebook contradicts the low-code preference.

Option D: If Condition is control-flow, not data movement.

fields.label: Send an email alert to the on-call engineer when any pipeline activity fails.
options: Copy activity — Copy supports a 'failure_email' parameter that sends an alert when the activity fails.
Notebook activity — write Python code in the notebook that sends an SMTP email on exception.
Send Email (Office 365 Outlook) activity — dedicated activity that sends a notification email via Outlook. Wire it to upstream activities' Failure outputs.
Dataflow activity — Dataflows have a built-in alerting layer that emails on refresh failure.
fields.correctAnswer: Send Email (Office 365 Outlook) activity — dedicated activity that sends a notification email via Outlook. Wire it to upstream activities' Failure outputs.
fields.rationale: Notifications are a dedicated activity, not a side feature of data activities. Send Email (Office 365 Outlook) is the standard pipeline-native notification path. The most common Junior confusion is putting notification logic INSIDE a notebook; pipeline-native activities are observable in pipeline run history and easier to maintain.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: No 'failure_email' parameter on Copy.

Option B: Notebook SMTP works but bypasses pipeline observability.

Option D: Dataflows don't have built-in email alerts.

fields.label: Call NordGrid's internal REST API to notify a downstream billing system that today's Silver load has completed successfully.
options: Copy activity — Copy can POST to HTTP endpoints when the destination is configured as REST.
Web activity — dedicated pipeline activity for HTTP calls (GET/POST/PUT) to internal or external REST APIs. Right tool for a notification call.
Notebook activity — write a few lines of Python with the requests library and POST to the billing API.
Dataflow activity — Dataflows include a Power Query Web.Contents step that can call REST APIs.
fields.correctAnswer: Web activity — dedicated pipeline activity for HTTP calls (GET/POST/PUT) to internal or external REST APIs. Right tool for a notification call.
fields.rationale: Web activity is the pipeline-native tool for HTTP calls. The most common Junior confusion is doing it from a notebook; while technically possible, putting a one-shot REST call in pipeline-level Web activity keeps it observable in pipeline run history alongside the data activities.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Copy is for data movement, not API calls.

Option C: Notebook works but bypasses pipeline observability.

Option D: Dataflows are for transformation; Web.Contents in Power Query is for ingestion, not pipeline notifications.

description.context: Configuring a Copy activity means filling SOURCE-side config (where the data comes from) and SINK-side config (where it goes). SOURCE: connection type (SFTP, HTTP, ADLS, on-prem DB, etc. — match the actual external system), format (CSV/JSON/Parquet — match what the external system produces), and path (which file or folder). SINK: connection type (Lakehouse, Warehouse), section for Lakehouses (Files for raw, Tables for managed Delta), path (date-based subdirectory like meter_exports/2026/03/10/ to preserve history), and write behavior (overwrite/append/preserve). For Bronze landing of daily exports, the design pattern is unique date-based paths (no overwrite), preserving every day's file as immutable history.
description.task: Predict the values for 4 configuration fields of NordGrid's Copy activity.
description.validationHint: The Copy activity has source-side config (connection type, format, path) and destination-side config (connection type, section, path, write behavior). Think about what each scenario detail implies for the correct config value.

fields.label: What is the correct SOURCE connection type for NordGrid's daily Copy activity?
options: Lakehouse — NordGrid stores everything in OneLake, so the Lakehouse is always the source for Copy activities.
SFTP — the data physically lives on an external SFTP server. Connection type matches the actual external transport.
Azure SQL Database — the default for raw ingestion, regardless of where the data actually lives.
HTTP — CSV files are transported over HTTP across the internet, so the connector is HTTP.
fields.correctAnswer: SFTP — the data physically lives on an external SFTP server. Connection type matches the actual external transport.
fields.rationale: Source connection type matches the actual external system (SFTP). The most common Junior confusion is mixing up source and destination — the Lakehouse is the SINK; the SFTP server is the SOURCE.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Lakehouse is the sink.

Option C: No 'Azure SQL default' rule.

Option D: SFTP and HTTP are different protocols with different connectors.

fields.label: What is the correct SOURCE file format for the Copy activity?
options: CSV — the scenario explicitly says meters_YYYY-MM-DD.csv. Source format matches what the external system produces.
Delta — Fabric standardizes on Delta, so the Copy activity should always read Delta sources.
Parquet — Parquet is the recommended analytical format and Copy should always pick it for performance.
JSON — modern data exchange uses JSON, so the source must be JSON regardless of file extension.
fields.correctAnswer: CSV — the scenario explicitly says meters_YYYY-MM-DD.csv. Source format matches what the external system produces.
fields.rationale: Source format matches what the external system produces — the file is .csv. The most common Junior confusion is conflating Fabric's storage preferences (Delta in Tables, Parquet for archival) with the source's actual format; you don't get to choose what arrives.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Delta is a destination format.

Option C: Parquet is destination/archival; doesn't match the source.

Option D: JSON contradicts the scenario's .csv filename.

fields.label: What is the correct DESTINATION for the raw copied file in the Bronze Lakehouse?
options: Tables section — landing in Tables makes the file immediately queryable via the auto-generated SQL endpoint, no notebook needed.
Files section — raw CSVs belong in unmanaged storage, written to a date-based path like Files/meter_exports/2026/03/10/. Standard Bronze landing pattern.
A new Warehouse dedicated to raw data — landing CSVs into a Warehouse provides immediate T-SQL access plus DML.
The semantic model — Power BI reads the raw CSV directly via the auto-generated semantic model.
fields.correctAnswer: Files section — raw CSVs belong in unmanaged storage, written to a date-based path like Files/meter_exports/2026/03/10/. Standard Bronze landing pattern.
fields.rationale: Bronze raw CSVs go in the Lakehouse Files section. The Tables section is for managed Delta only — CSVs don't qualify and the SQL endpoint won't see them. The most common Junior confusion is hoping for instant SQL queryability by landing in Tables; CSVs must be promoted to Delta by a notebook before the endpoint can read them.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Tables is for Delta, not raw CSV.

Option C: Warehouses don't have a Files section.

Option D: Semantic model sits on Tables, not raw files.

fields.label: What DESTINATION file behavior should the Copy activity use, given that each daily file lands at a unique date-based path and previous days' files must be preserved?
options: Overwrite — replace the entire Bronze Lakehouse contents each day so only today's file remains.
Write to a unique date-based path (meter_exports/2026/03/10/) — each day's file lands in its own folder, so previous days are preserved and no overwrite is needed.
Append all days into a single concatenated file (meter_exports/readings.csv) so the Silver notebook can read 'all data' from one location.
Merge with existing data — Copy activity deduplicates by primary key during write.
fields.correctAnswer: Write to a unique date-based path (meter_exports/2026/03/10/) — each day's file lands in its own folder, so previous days are preserved and no overwrite is needed.
fields.rationale: Bronze landing uses date-based paths so each day's file is immutable history. No overwrite, no append, no merge. The most common Junior confusion is using overwrite (destroys history) or single-file append (complicates incremental reads); date-based folders make Bronze replayable and traceable.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Overwrite destroys archive.

Option C: Append-to-single-file complicates incremental processing.

Option D: Copy doesn't deduplicate; that's Silver-stage logic.

tasks.title: Write a Parameterized NordGrid Notebook

description.context: NordGrid's Silver notebook is parameterized: the daily pipeline passes two parameters to it — processing_date (the date of the data to process) and region_filter (limiting processing to one region for incremental runs). In Fabric, a pipeline's Notebook activity injects these parameters into a special parameters cell at the top of the notebook. Your job is to write the code BELOW the parameters cell: code that reads the raw data, filters by the parameters, and produces the Silver DataFrame. The key rule: your code must REFERENCE the params dict, not hardcode the date or region values. That way, the same notebook works for any day and any region the pipeline passes in.
description.task: Read F7_data_readings.csv into df_raw. Filter df_raw to rows where date equals params['processing_date'] AND region equals params['region_filter']. Store the filtered DataFrame in df_silver. Store the row count in silver_row_count. The scaffold pre-populates params with the simulated pipeline injection: {'processing_date': '2026-03-10', 'region_filter': 'EAST'}.
description.validationHint: Use col('date') == params['processing_date'] and col('region') == params['region_filter']. For the specific test params (2026-03-10, EAST), there are exactly 2 matching rows (M-0013 and M-0014). Do not hardcode '2026-03-10' or 'EAST' in your filter — reference the params dict so the notebook is reusable.

starterScaffold.content:
# F7 Lesson 8: parameterized notebooks. In Fabric, the pipeline's Notebook activity
# injects parameters into a parameters cell at the top of the notebook. In this local
# practice, the `params` dict below simulates that injection — pretend it was written
# by the pipeline, not by you.
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import col

spark = SparkSession.builder \
    .appName('nordgrid-parameterized-silver') \
    .master('local[*]') \
    .getOrCreate()

# Simulated pipeline parameter injection (this cell would be auto-generated by Fabric):
params = {
    'processing_date': '2026-03-10',
    'region_filter': 'EAST'
}
print(f"Parameters injected by pipeline: {params}")

df_raw = spark.read.csv('F7_data_readings.csv', header=True, inferSchema=True)
print(f"Raw rows loaded: {df_raw.count()}")

# YOUR SOLUTION BELOW
# Filter df_raw to rows where:
#   date equals params['processing_date']
#   AND region equals params['region_filter']
# Store the filtered DataFrame in df_silver.
# Store the row count in silver_row_count.
# IMPORTANT: your filter MUST reference params['processing_date'] and params['region_filter'] —
# do not hardcode the literal values. This is what makes the notebook reusable across days.




# YOUR SOLUTION ABOVE

# Verification (do not modify)
print(f"Silver rows for {params['processing_date']} / {params['region_filter']}: {silver_row_count}")
df_silver.show()

assertions.description: silver_row_count equals 2 (M-0013 and M-0014 match 2026-03-10 + EAST)
All rows in df_silver have date == 2026-03-10
All rows in df_silver have region == EAST

tasks.partialCredit: 5 independent assertions. Each passed assertion earns 1/5 credit.

description.context: Pipeline activities run based on DEPENDENCIES that pass or block based on the upstream activity's outcome. The four dependency types: SUCCESS (run only if upstream succeeded), FAILURE (run only if upstream failed), COMPLETION (run when upstream finishes regardless of success/failure), and SKIPPED (run only if upstream itself was skipped). When a dependency isn't met, the activity is SKIPPED (not failed, not run). Skipped activities cascade — if A skips, B that depends on A's success skips too. PIPELINE STATUS rolls up: Succeeded if every activity that RAN succeeded; Failed if any activity that ran failed. Skipped activities don't fail the pipeline, but failed ones do — even if a downstream notify-on-failure activity ran successfully (sending an alert is acknowledgment, not recovery).
description.task: Predict the outcome of each scenario.
description.validationHint: Dependency types: SUCCESS means 'run only if the upstream activity succeeded.' FAILURE means 'run only if the upstream activity failed.' If an activity is skipped because its dependency was not met, the pipeline treats that activity as not-run (not failed). The overall pipeline status is 'Succeeded' if all activities that ran succeeded, or 'Failed' if any activity that ran failed.

fields.label: Scenario 1: copy_bronze succeeds, transform_silver succeeds, transform_gold succeeds. What is the outcome?
options: All 4 activities run; pipeline status: Succeeded. Every activity in a pipeline runs to completion regardless of dependency type.
3 activities run (copy_bronze, transform_silver, transform_gold). notify_failure is SKIPPED because its FAILURE dependency on copy_bronze was not met. Pipeline: Succeeded.
All 4 activities run; pipeline status: Failed because notify_failure sent an unexpected email even though no failure occurred.
Only copy_bronze runs; the other activities are blocked by a dependency cycle introduced when notify_failure references copy_bronze.
fields.correctAnswer: 3 activities run (copy_bronze, transform_silver, transform_gold). notify_failure is SKIPPED because its FAILURE dependency on copy_bronze was not met. Pipeline: Succeeded.
fields.rationale: When the upstream succeeds, FAILURE-dependent activities are SKIPPED (not run, not failed). The pipeline status only considers activities that RAN — all three succeeded, so the pipeline is Succeeded. The most common Junior confusion is treating a skipped activity as a failure; skipped is its own category that doesn't count against the pipeline.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Skipped activities don't run.

Option C: Skipped activities don't send emails.

Option D: No dependency cycle exists in this graph.

fields.label: Scenario 2: copy_bronze FAILS (SFTP credential expired). What is the outcome?
options: copy_bronze fails; transform_silver and transform_gold run anyway because pipeline activities are independent; pipeline: Failed.
copy_bronze fails; transform_silver SKIPS (SUCCESS dep unmet); transform_gold SKIPS (cascades from skipped upstream); notify_failure RUNS (its FAILURE dep is met); pipeline: Failed.
copy_bronze fails; Fabric auto-retries it 3 times by default and the pipeline eventually succeeds without notify_failure firing.
copy_bronze fails but notify_failure runs successfully, which 'recovers' the pipeline; status: Succeeded because the failure was handled.
fields.correctAnswer: copy_bronze fails; transform_silver SKIPS (SUCCESS dep unmet); transform_gold SKIPS (cascades from skipped upstream); notify_failure RUNS (its FAILURE dep is met); pipeline: Failed.
fields.rationale: Skipping cascades: when copy_bronze fails, transform_silver skips (SUCCESS unmet), and transform_gold skips because its upstream (transform_silver) was skipped. notify_failure RUNS because its FAILURE-on-copy_bronze dep IS met. The pipeline is Failed because copy_bronze failed; sending an alert email doesn't recover from that. The most common Junior confusion is thinking the email 'fixes' the pipeline status; alerting is acknowledgment, not recovery.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Skipped activities don't run.

Option C: No automatic retry without explicit config.

Option D: Notification is not recovery.

fields.label: Scenario 3: copy_bronze succeeds, transform_silver FAILS (bug in PySpark code), transform_gold has not started yet. What is the outcome?
options: copy_bronze runs; transform_silver fails; transform_gold SKIPS (SUCCESS dep unmet); notify_failure SKIPS (its dep is on copy_bronze FAILURE, not transform_silver). Pipeline: Failed. No alert sent.
copy_bronze runs; transform_silver fails; transform_gold runs anyway because it is a separate activity; pipeline: Failed.
copy_bronze runs; transform_silver fails; notify_failure runs because notify_failure triggers on ANY upstream failure in the pipeline; pipeline: Failed.
All four activities run; pipeline: Succeeded because notify_failure detected the issue and the system gracefully recovered.
fields.correctAnswer: copy_bronze runs; transform_silver fails; transform_gold SKIPS (SUCCESS dep unmet); notify_failure SKIPS (its dep is on copy_bronze FAILURE, not transform_silver). Pipeline: Failed. No alert sent.
fields.rationale: Dependencies are PER-ACTIVITY, not per-pipeline. notify_failure only fires when copy_bronze (its specific dependency target) fails — a transform_silver failure does NOT trigger it. The scenario reveals an alerting GAP. The most common Junior confusion is thinking 'on-failure' alerting is global; it's wired to specific upstream activities and you need separate alerts for each critical path.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: SUCCESS dep blocks transform_gold.

Option C: Dep is on copy_bronze specifically, not 'any failure'.

Option D: Activity-level failure rolls up to pipeline failure.

fields.label: NordGrid's team wants transform_silver to run EVEN IF copy_bronze fails — for example, to reprocess yesterday's Bronze data when today's ingestion fails. What dependency type should they change?
options: Change SUCCESS to COMPLETION — runs whenever copy_bronze FINISHES (success OR failure). The dependency type designed for exactly this 'run regardless of outcome' case.
Change SUCCESS to FAILURE — runs only when copy_bronze fails. Inverts the path; the normal-day case stops working.
Remove the dependency entirely — transform_silver runs in parallel with copy_bronze, racing the data load.
Add a second copy_bronze activity as a retry and chain transform_silver to the retry; keep the original SUCCESS dep.
fields.correctAnswer: Change SUCCESS to COMPLETION — runs whenever copy_bronze FINISHES (success OR failure). The dependency type designed for exactly this 'run regardless of outcome' case.
fields.rationale: COMPLETION is the dependency type that fires on EITHER success or failure. It exists for cases where the downstream wants 'run after upstream finishes, no matter the outcome'. The most common Junior confusion is reaching for FAILURE (which inverts the normal path) or removing the dep (which creates a race); COMPLETION is the exact tool.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: FAILURE inverts the path; breaks normal day.

Option C: No dep creates a race condition.

Option D: Adds complexity when COMPLETION exists for this.

description.context: Pipeline triggers control WHEN a pipeline runs. Two trigger families: SCHEDULED (hourly/daily/weekly/monthly with a specific time) and MANUAL (no schedule; runs only when a human clicks Run). The choice rule is simple: match the trigger cadence to the SOURCE's update cadence. Daily file arrival = daily trigger; continuously-arriving telemetry = hourly trigger; weekly upstream refresh = weekly trigger; one-off reprocessing job = manual trigger (never schedule a one-off, because the schedule will keep firing). Mismatched cadence wastes capacity (running too often) or breaks SLAs (running too rarely).
description.task: For each NordGrid data flow, select the correct trigger configuration.
description.validationHint: Match the cadence of the data arrival to the trigger cadence. If source data arrives daily, the pipeline runs daily. If the pipeline is a one-off reprocessing job, it uses a manual trigger. If the source emits continuously, the pipeline runs hourly or on a streaming schedule.

fields.label: NordGrid's external SFTP server publishes the daily meter CSV at 01:30 UTC every morning. The pipeline must run after the file arrives but before the 06:00 UTC analyst workday begins.
options: Hourly trigger starting at 00:00 UTC — guarantees the pipeline catches the file no matter when it arrives.
Daily trigger at 02:00 UTC — fires once per day, 30 minutes after file arrival, completing before 06:00. Cadence matches source.
Weekly trigger on Monday at 02:00 UTC — schedule the load weekly to batch processing.
Manual trigger — engineer logs in each morning and runs the pipeline as part of on-call rotation.
fields.correctAnswer: Daily trigger at 02:00 UTC — fires once per day, 30 minutes after file arrival, completing before 06:00. Cadence matches source.
fields.rationale: Daily file arrival = daily trigger, scheduled after arrival and before SLA. The most common Junior confusion is over-running (hourly when source is daily wastes capacity) or under-running (manual is operationally fragile).
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Hourly wastes 23 runs per day for a daily source.

Option C: Weekly misses 6 of 7 days.

Option D: Manual is unsustainable for daily prod.

fields.label: NordGrid's SCADA telemetry from wind turbines arrives continuously as new files every 10 minutes. The pipeline must process the latest files frequently enough that the operations dashboard is never more than 1 hour stale.
options: Hourly trigger — fires every hour, keeps the dashboard within the 1-hour SLA, and matches the source's continuous cadence at minimal capacity cost.
Daily trigger — once per day at midnight; aligns with NordGrid's normal daily ETL window.
Weekly trigger — process all telemetry weekly to keep cost low.
Manual trigger — operations team runs the pipeline manually when they notice the dashboard is stale.
fields.correctAnswer: Hourly trigger — fires every hour, keeps the dashboard within the 1-hour SLA, and matches the source's continuous cadence at minimal capacity cost.
fields.rationale: 1-hour staleness SLA = hourly trigger (or finer). Anything daily/weekly/manual breaks the SLA. The most common Junior confusion is reaching for daily as the 'standard' cadence; trigger cadence must match the freshness REQUIREMENT, not the team's habit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B/C: Both exceed the 1-hour SLA.

Option D: Manual breaks the SLA the moment the team isn't watching.

fields.label: NordGrid's substation reference table (static metadata — 200 rows) needs to be refreshed from an upstream operations system, but the upstream system only updates the reference data on Mondays.
options: Hourly trigger — refresh frequently to be safe; capacity overhead is negligible for 200 rows.
Daily trigger — refresh every morning regardless of whether the upstream changed.
Weekly on Monday evening, after the upstream update — match the source's cadence exactly. No wasted runs, source freshness preserved.
Manual trigger — engineer runs it whenever they notice the substation list looks outdated.
fields.correctAnswer: Weekly on Monday evening, after the upstream update — match the source's cadence exactly. No wasted runs, source freshness preserved.
fields.rationale: When the source updates weekly, the trigger should run weekly — and AFTER the source update, not before. The most common Junior confusion is over-running ('it's cheap, just refresh hourly'); even cheap pipelines accumulate run-history clutter and obscure real failures.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Hourly wastes 167 runs per week.

Option B: Daily wastes 6 of 7 runs.

Option D: Manual is operationally fragile.

fields.label: NordGrid's team needs to reprocess 6 months of historical meter data after discovering a bug in last year's Silver transformation logic. The reprocessing is a one-time operation expected to run for 4 hours on a weekend.
options: Daily trigger — schedule it for tomorrow morning so the team can leave it running unattended.
Weekly trigger — schedule it for Saturday so it runs again next Saturday automatically.
Manual trigger — engineer runs ONCE on Saturday and verifies completion. One-off jobs should never use a recurring schedule.
Hourly trigger — let it fire repeatedly to maximize chances of completing if any single run fails.
fields.correctAnswer: Manual trigger — engineer runs ONCE on Saturday and verifies completion. One-off jobs should never use a recurring schedule.
fields.rationale: One-time reprocessing = manual trigger, every time. Scheduling a one-off creates a footgun: the schedule keeps firing and re-runs the reprocessing on subsequent days/weeks, potentially corrupting data. The most common Junior confusion is using schedules for everything; manual triggers exist specifically for human-initiated one-shots.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Daily would re-run forever after the one-off.

Option B: Weekly would re-run every Saturday.

Option D: Hourly creates concurrent runs and chaos.

tasks.title: Design NordGrid's Complete Daily Pipeline

description.context:
NordGrid's platform team is authoring the specification for the daily pipeline (pl_nordgrid_daily). The specification is a structured document that the platform team versions in Git: it lists the pipeline name, the parameters, the schedule, and every activity with its type, dependencies, and key configuration. New engineers read this specification to understand how the pipeline is assembled before opening it in the portal canvas.

You are writing this specification as a Python dictionary. No Fabric runtime is required — this is pure Python data structure construction that synthesizes every F7 concept: activity types (Lesson 3, 4, 5), dependencies (Lesson 6), scheduling (Lesson 7), and parameters (Lesson 8). The pipeline has 3 activities in sequence plus one failure-branch activity.
description.task:
Build a Python dictionary called nordgrid_daily_pipeline with these top-level keys:

  - name: the pipeline name 'pl_nordgrid_daily'
  - schedule: a nested dict with keys frequency ('daily'), time ('02:00'), timezone ('UTC')
  - parameters: a nested dict with one parameter named 'processing_date' of type 'string'
  - activities: a list of exactly 4 activity dicts, each with the keys name, type, depends_on

The 4 activities are:

  (1) name='copy_bronze_meters', type='Copy', depends_on=[]

synthesisNotes.rationale: This task synthesizes every F7 concept into a single structured specification. Each activity tests a different lesson: copy_bronze_meters tests Copy activity understanding (Lesson 3), transform_silver and transform_gold test Notebook activity plus dependency chaining (Lessons 4, 6), notify_failure tests the FAILURE dependency condition (Lesson 6). The schedule tests Lesson 7, and the parameters section tests Lesson 8. A student who recalls individual lessons in isolation cannot complete this task — they must assemble them into a coherent pipeline. The 9 independent assertions provide fine-grained partial credit so students earn credit for the parts they got right even if they misconfigure one activity.

selfCheck.foundationModuleException: Not applied. F7 is Essential Operations phase. The practice set is template-heavy (5 of 6 tasks use templates or dict construction) because pipelines are a UI concept — most F7 knowledge is about which activity, which dependency, which schedule, rather than about writing code. The single code task tests the notebook-side of pipeline integration (parameterized notebooks). Task type mix (2 concept_identification + 2 output_prediction + 1 write_the_code + 1 synthesis_pipeline) is within §4.2 per-type limits.
selfCheck.theoryPracticeBoundary: The theory walks through NordGrid's daily pipeline in Lessons 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 10 using consistent examples (pl_ingest_meters, the Bronze-to-Silver flow, the 02:00 UTC schedule). The practice tests application: Task 1 uses NordGrid steps the theory does not fully enumerate (the Send Email notification and Web API call are adaptations). Task 2 tests configuration-level decisions the theory explains conceptually but does not walk through as a fill-in-the-blanks exercise. Task 4 creates failure scenarios the theory describes briefly — the student must trace dependency logic through specific failure modes rather than recalling the nominal success path. Task 5 adds scenarios beyond the theory's daily example. Task 6 builds the specification the theory walks through, but as a structured Python data structure the student assembles from scratch.
selfCheck.crossModuleNotes: This practice set builds on knowledge from earlier modules: F2's workspace and item naming (pl_ prefix for pipelines), F4's Lakehouse Files/Tables distinction (Task 2 field F3), F5's pre-configured spark and Lakehouse access (Task 3), and F6's transformation patterns (Task 3 applies a filter like the ones in F6). None of these are tested directly — they are context. F7 adds the orchestration layer on top: which activity runs what, when, and in what order. F8 (Dataflows Gen2) is referenced in Task 1 field F3 only at the level F7 Lesson 5 introduces (the Dataflow activity as a pipeline building block) — detailed Dataflow knowledge is not required and is covered in F8.
selfCheck.datasetNotes: One small dataset (15 rows) used only by Task 3's parameterized filter. Tasks 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are entirely template-based or pure Python data structure construction and require no CSV files.
